mainTopic: Being judged by one's end: the בן סורר ומורה and the burglar (בא במחתרת), and whether a burglar must pay for or return what he took
overview: The גמרא opens with a ברייתא from רבי יוסי הגלילי. He explains that a בן סורר ומורה is not punished for one meal; the Torah sees that his path will lead to robbery, so it is better that he die innocent. A new משנה teaches that a burglar who tunnels in (הבא במחתרת) is also judged by his likely end, and that he pays for a barrel he breaks only if killing him would be forbidden. רבא explains that a burglar expects the owner to defend his money and is ready to kill him, so the owner may kill him first. רב rules that such a burglar keeps the vessels he took, because he 'acquired them with his blood.' רבא first limits this to broken items, then admits רב meant even items that still exist, and explains why he himself disagrees: paying for accidents is not ownership, just like a borrower. The גמרא challenges רב from the משנה's wording, which stays a קשיא. It challenges רבא from a ברייתא about stealing a purse on שבת, and answers it. A story shows רבא refusing to take back his own stolen rams out of respect for רב's ruling. Finally, two ברייתות read 'if the sun has risen upon him' in opposite ways for a homeowner who is unsure of the burglar's intent; the answer begins at the end of the amud and continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Is he really stoned just for one meal?
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוסי הגלילי asks, as a pointed question, whether the Torah would really stone a boy just for eating some meat and drinking some wine.
steps.simpleTranslation: GEMARA: A ברייתא teaches: רבי יוסי הגלילי says: Is it only because this boy ate a תרטימר of meat and drank half a לוג of Italian wine that the Torah says he should be brought to court and stoned?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא where רבי יוסי הגלילי raises a pointed question about the בן סורר ומורה. He is setting up his own answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The amounts named here are exactly the ones the משנה gave as the act that makes a boy a בן סורר ומורה. רבי יוסי הגלילי points out that this act alone seems far too small for the death penalty. That gap must be explained.

keyTerms.meaning: A measure of weight, the amount of meat named in the משנה
Half a לוג, a liquid measure

phrases.english: GEMARA: It is taught in a ברייתא:
Rabbi Yosei HaGelili says:
Is it really because this one ate
a tarteimar of meat
and drank half a log of Italian wine
that the Torah said
he should go out to court to be stoned?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens the גמרא on the end of the previous משנה about בן סורר ומורה.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What is the real reason behind the harsh punishment of the בן סורר ומורה?

steps.title: The Torah sees where his path will end
steps.stepSummary: The Torah looks ahead. This boy will use up his father's money, and when he cannot feed his habits he will turn to robbing people at the crossroads.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, the Torah saw into the final mindset of the בן סורר ומורה. In the end he will use up his father's property, look for what he is used to and not find it, and go out to the crossroads and rob people.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוסי הגלילי answers his own question. The boy is punished because of where his behavior is clearly heading.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The punishment is not really for the meal. It is for the future his habits will lead to: wasting his father's wealth and then robbing, and likely killing, people. This idea is called נידון על שם סופו, being judged by one's end.

keyTerms.meaning: To the end of his mind, meaning where his thinking will lead him
Robs, acts as a highway robber

steps.whyThisMatters: This explains the whole parsha of בן סורר ומורה. It also sets up the משנה that follows, which uses the same idea of being judged by one's end.

phrases.english: Rather, the Torah reached the end of the mindset
of the stubborn and rebellious son,
that in the end he will use up his father's property
and will look for what he is used to and not find it,
and he will go out to the crossroads
and rob people.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question raised in step 1.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: He is punished for where his behavior will lead, not for the meal itself.

steps.title: Better to die innocent than guilty
steps.stepSummary: The Torah prefers that he die now while still innocent, because the death of the wicked is good for them and for the world.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Torah said: Let him die innocent and not die guilty. The death of the wicked is good for them and good for the world. The death of the righteous is bad for them and bad for the world.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא explains why it is better to execute him now instead of waiting for his crimes.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If he dies now, he dies before committing robbery and murder, so his record stays clean. That helps him, and it also protects the world from the harm he would do. A righteous person is the opposite: his life helps everyone, so his death is a loss.

phrases.english: The Torah said:
Let him die innocent and not die guilty,
because the death of the wicked
is good for them and good for the world,
and for the righteous
it is bad for them and bad for the world.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמְרָה תּוֹרָה: יָמוּת זַכַּאי וְאַל יָמוּת חַיָּיב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds the reason why executing him now is a kindness.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: It is better for the בן סורר ומורה to die now while innocent than later after committing crimes.

steps.title: More things that help or hurt the wicked and the righteous
steps.stepSummary: A list follows. Sleep and wine help when the wicked have them and hurt when the righteous do. Quiet is the reverse. Scattering helps when the wicked are scattered and hurts when the righteous are.
steps.simpleTranslation: Sleep and wine for the wicked are good for them and the world. For the righteous they are bad for them and the world. Quiet for the wicked is bad for them and the world. For the righteous it is good for them and the world. Scattering of the wicked is good for them and the world. Scattering of the righteous is bad for them and the world.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא adds more pairs in the same pattern as the line about death.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When the wicked sleep, drink, or are spread apart, they do less harm. When the righteous are in those states, they do less good. Quiet and calm are the opposite: they let the wicked plot together, while the righteous use them to do good.
steps.whatToRemember: The בן סורר ומורה is judged by where he is heading. His early death is seen as good for him and for the world.
steps.confusionAlert: Watch the order. For quiet (שקט), it is bad for the wicked and good for the righteous, the reverse of the other items.

phrases.english: Sleep and wine for the wicked
are good for them and good for the world;
for the righteous, bad for them and bad for the world.

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁקֶט לָרְשָׁעִים – רַע לָהֶם וְרַע לָעוֹלָם,
phrases.english: Quiet for the wicked is bad for them and bad for the world,
and for the righteous, good for them and good for the world.

phrases.aramaic: פִּיזּוּר לָרְשָׁעִים – הֲנָאָה לָהֶם וַהֲנָאָה לָעוֹלָם,
phrases.english: Scattering for the wicked is good for them and good for the world,
and for the righteous, bad for them and bad for the world.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Extends the pattern from step 3 to more examples.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: What limits the wicked helps the world. What limits the righteous harms it.

steps.title: The burglar is judged by his end
steps.stepSummary: A new משנה teaches that a burglar who tunnels into a house is also judged by what he would likely do in the end.
steps.simpleTranslation: MISHNAH: One who comes in by tunneling (a burglar) is judged on account of his end.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It applies the same idea, being judged by one's end, to a burglar.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The Torah allows the homeowner to kill a burglar who breaks in. This משנה explains that he is treated as if he were already a killer, because that is where the break-in is likely to lead.

keyTerms.meaning: One who comes in by tunneling, a burglar breaking in
Judged on account of his end

phrases.english: MISHNAH: One who comes in through tunneling
phrases.notes: This is the burglar from שמות 22:1.

phrases.english: is judged on account of his end.

steps.triggerLanguage: הַבָּא בַּמַּחְתֶּרֶת נִידּוֹן עַל שֵׁם סוֹפוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: New משנה that uses the same idea as בן סורר ומורה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A burglar is treated according to what he would likely end up doing.

steps.title: The burglar who breaks a barrel
steps.stepSummary: If a burglar breaks a barrel while breaking in, whether he pays depends on whether killing him would be allowed.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he was breaking in and broke a barrel: if killing him would be murder, he must pay. If killing him would be allowed, he does not pay.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה adds a money case connected to the burglar.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the homeowner was allowed to kill him, the burglar was in a state of deserving death. Someone facing death does not also pay for damage. If killing him would be murder, for example a father breaking into his son's home, he is a normal person and must pay for the barrel.

keyTerms.meaning: Blood, here meaning guilt for killing him

steps.confusionAlert: Here 'he has blood' (יש לו דמים) means that killing him would count as murder. It does not mean the burglar is guilty.

phrases.english: If he was coming in through tunneling
and broke the barrel,
if he has blood, he is liable,
phrases.notes: Meaning the homeowner would be guilty if he killed him, so the burglar is treated as a normal person.

phrases.english: if he has no blood, he is exempt.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָיָה בָּא בַּמַּחְתֶּרֶת וְשָׁבַר אֶת הֶחָבִית
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a practical money ruling for the burglar.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A burglar who may be killed does not pay for the barrel. One who may not be killed does pay.

steps.title: רבא asks why a burglar may be killed
steps.stepSummary: רבא asks for the reason behind the law of the burglar.
steps.simpleTranslation: GEMARA: רבא said: What is the reason for the law of the burglar?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens with רבא asking why the Torah allows killing a burglar. He is setting up his own explanation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה said the burglar is judged by his end, but did not explain why we assume he would kill. רבא is going to fill in that reasoning.

phrases.english: GEMARA: Rava said:
What is the reason for the burglar?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens the גמרא on the new משנה.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why is the homeowner allowed to kill a burglar?

steps.title: A person defends his money, so the burglar plans to kill
steps.stepSummary: People do not stand by while their money is taken. The burglar therefore plans to kill the owner if he resists, and the Torah says to kill first someone who comes to kill you.
steps.simpleTranslation: There is a presumption that a person does not hold himself back when his money is at stake. This burglar must have said: 'If I go in, he will stand against me and not let me, and if he stands against me, I will kill him.' And the Torah said: If someone comes to kill you, get up early and kill him first.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives his reason. The burglar is assumed to be ready to kill, so the homeowner may defend himself first.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The reasoning has three links. First, owners fight for their money (a חזקה). Second, so the burglar comes ready to kill. Third, so he counts as a רודף, someone coming to kill, and the Torah allows killing him first.

keyTerms.meaning: A presumption about how people normally act
Holds himself back when his money is at stake
Get up early and kill him first

steps.whatToRemember: The burglar may be killed because we assume he is ready to kill the owner who defends his money. That makes him someone coming to kill.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is the source for the הלכה of self-defense against a person coming to kill you.

phrases.aramaic: חֲזָקָה אֵין אָדָם מַעֲמִיד עַצְמוֹ עַל מָמוֹנוֹ,
phrases.english: There is a presumption that a person does not hold himself back regarding his money,
phrases.notes: Meaning nobody quietly watches his money get stolen; he will fight back.

phrases.english: and this one surely said to himself:
If I go in, he will stand against me
and will not let me,
and if he stands against me, I will kill him.
And the Torah said:
If he comes to kill you, get up early and kill him first.

steps.triggerLanguage: חֲזָקָה אֵין אָדָם מַעֲמִיד עַצְמוֹ עַל מָמוֹנוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רבא's question from step 7.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Because owners defend their money, the burglar comes ready to kill. The Torah allows killing first someone who comes to kill.

steps.title: רב: The tunneling burglar who took vessels is exempt
steps.stepSummary: רב rules that a burglar who tunneled in, took vessels and left is exempt, because he 'acquired them with blood.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רב says: if someone broke in through tunneling, took vessels and left, he is exempt. Why? He acquired them with his blood.
steps.whatsHappening: רב gives a new rule: a tunneling burglar who got away with vessels does not have to pay. His reason is that he 'bought' them with his life.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When he broke in, the owner was allowed to kill him, so he was putting his life on the line. Because his life was at stake, he is free from the lighter penalty of paying for what he took. This builds on the idea from Step 6 about the broken barrel.

keyTerms.meaning: Exempt; does not have to pay
He acquired them with blood, meaning by risking his life

phrases.english: Rav says:
One who comes in through tunneling
and took vessels and left — is exempt.
What is the reason?
He acquired them with blood.
phrases.notes: He risked his life breaking in, since the owner could have killed him.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב: הַבָּא בַּמַּחְתֶּרֶת וְנָטַל כֵּלִים וְיָצָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Takes the burglar's life-risk from Steps 6 and 8 and applies it to items he took and left with.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A tunneling burglar who took vessels and left is exempt, because he acquired them by risking his life.

steps.title: רבא limits רב to broken items
steps.stepSummary: רבא says רב's ruling makes sense only when the vessels were broken and are gone, not when the burglar still has them.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא says: רב's statement is reasonable where he broke the vessels so they no longer exist. But if he just took them, it does not apply.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא narrows רב's rule. The burglar is exempt from paying for broken items, but he must give back items he still has.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There is a difference between paying money for something destroyed and returning an item that still exists. רבא thinks the life-risk only frees the burglar from paying, not from returning the actual stolen object.

keyTerms.meaning: It makes sense; it is reasonable

steps.confusionAlert: At this point רבא is trying to read רב narrowly, as talking only about items that no longer exist. In step 11 רבא himself takes this back and admits רב meant even items that still exist. By step 13, רבא ends up disagreeing with רב's reasoning rather than explaining it.

phrases.english: Rava says:
Rav's statement is reasonable
where he broke them, so they no longer exist,
but if he took them — not.
phrases.notes: If the vessels still exist, he has to give them back.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָבָא: מִסְתַּבְּרָא מִילְּתֵיהּ דְּרַב בְּשֶׁשִּׁיבֵּר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits רב's ruling from Step 9 to vessels that were destroyed.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב's exemption applies only to broken vessels. Vessels that still exist must be returned.

steps.title: No! רב said it even when he simply took the vessels
steps.stepSummary: רבא takes back his own limit and swears that רב said the burglar is exempt even when he took the vessels and they still exist.
steps.simpleTranslation: But by God! רב said it even when he took them.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא withdraws the limit he just put on רב. He swears that רב's rule covered even items that still exist. The next step gives רב's reasoning.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the previous step, רבא suggested that רב meant only broken items. Now רבא admits that רב made no such distinction, so by רב's view even items still in the burglar's hands belong to him. In step 13, רבא will explain why he himself disagrees.

keyTerms.meaning: But by God! A strong exclamation of disagreement

phrases.english: But by God!
phrases.notes: רבא says this like an oath, taking back the limit he just suggested.

phrases.english: Rav said: even if he took —

steps.relationToPreviousStep: רבא retracts his own narrowing from Step 10.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: רבא's limiting of רב to broken vessels
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: רב's ruling covered even vessels that were taken and still exist.

steps.title: Proof: the stolen items count as in the burglar's possession
steps.stepSummary: When killing the burglar is forbidden and the items are lost by accident, he must pay. So the items are in his possession, and here too they are his.
steps.simpleTranslation: For where there is blood for him and the items were lost by accident, he is liable. So the items are in his possession. Here too, they are in his possession.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives the reasoning behind רב's broad ruling. It points to a known case where the burglar pays even for accidents, which shows the items are counted as his.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If killing the burglar would be murder, such as a father stealing from his son, he pays even for accidental loss. That shows the Torah treats the stolen items as being in his possession. So in the regular case, where he risked his life, the items should belong to him outright, even if they still exist.

keyTerms.meaning: There is blood for him, meaning killing him would count as murder
They were lost or damaged by accident

phrases.english: for where there is blood for him
phrases.notes: A case where killing him is not allowed, such as a father stealing from his son.

phrases.english: and they were lost by accident, he is liable.
Apparently they stand in his possession.
Here too, they stand in his possession.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּהָא יֵשׁ לוֹ דָּמִים וְנֶאֶנְסוּ, חַיָּיב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Backs up Step 11's claim that רב meant even items that still exist.
steps.raayaObject: The broad reading of רב: even items that still exist belong to the burglar.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The rule that a burglar who may not be killed pays even for accidental loss, which shows the items are in his possession.

steps.title: Rejected: liability for accidents is not ownership, like a borrower
steps.stepSummary: The proof fails. The Torah put the items in the burglar's possession only for paying for accidents, not for ownership, just like a borrower.
steps.simpleTranslation: But it is not so. When the Torah placed them in his possession, it was only for accidents. For ownership, they stay with their owner, just like with a borrower.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא disagrees with רב's reasoning from Step 12. Paying for accidents does not mean the burglar owns the items.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A borrower must pay if the borrowed item is lost by accident, yet it still belongs to the lender. In the same way, the burglar's duty to pay for accidents does not make him the owner. So רבא does not accept רב's reasoning: items that still exist go back to their owner, even though רב himself ruled otherwise.

keyTerms.meaning: The Merciful One, meaning the Torah

steps.whatToRemember: Being responsible for an item, even for accidents, is not the same as owning it. The proof is the borrower, who pays for accidents but never owns what he borrowed.

phrases.english: But it is not so;
when the Merciful One placed them in his possession,
it was regarding accidents,
but regarding ownership —
they stand in the possession of their owner,
just as with a borrower.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְלָא הִיא, כִּי אוֹקְמִינְהוּ רַחֲמָנָא בִּרְשׁוּתֵיהּ לְעִנְיַן אֳנָסִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: רבא rejects רב's reasoning from Step 12, so רבא himself holds that items that still exist must be returned.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The proof that the items belong to the burglar
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: Being responsible for accidents is not ownership, as the borrower shows.

steps.title: Challenge to רב from the משנה about the barrel
steps.stepSummary: The משנה exempts the burglar only when he broke the barrel. That implies that if he took it, he would not be exempt, which goes against רב.
steps.simpleTranslation: We learned: if he came through tunneling and broke the barrel, he is liable if there is blood for him and exempt if there is not. The reason is that he broke it. But if he took it, he would not be exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב using the משנה from Step 6. Since the משנה talks only about breaking the barrel, it seems that taking it would not be exempt.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא reads the משנה carefully: it chose the case of breaking for a reason. That suggests taking an item that still exists is different, and the burglar would have to return it. This clashes with רב's ruling that a burglar who took vessels is exempt.

keyTerms.meaning: But this other case (an inference from what was said)

steps.confusionAlert: The challenge works by looking at what the משנה left out. It mentions only breaking, so the גמרא concludes that taking would be different.

phrases.english: We learned:
If he came through tunneling and broke the barrel,
if there is blood for him — liable,
if there is no blood for him — exempt.
The reason is that he broke it,
that when there is no blood for him he is exempt.
But if he took it — not.
phrases.notes: He would not be exempt; he would have to give the barrel back.

steps.triggerLanguage: תְּנַן: בָּא בַּמַּחְתֶּרֶת וְשִׁיבֵּר אֶת הֶחָבִית
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns from the debate over how to read רב to a direct challenge against רב from the משנה.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's ruling that a burglar who took vessels is exempt (Step 9)
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה exempts the burglar only for breaking the barrel, which implies that taking it would not be exempt.

steps.title: The משנה's 'broke' teaches the opposite case
steps.stepSummary: The burglar is exempt even if he took the barrel. The משנה says 'broke' to teach that when killing him is forbidden, he must pay even for a barrel he broke.
steps.simpleTranslation: Really, the burglar is exempt even if he just took the barrel. The משנה says 'he broke the barrel' to teach us something else: when killing him would be forbidden, he must pay even though he broke it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge from step 14 and defends רב. It says the word 'broke' in the משנה is not there to limit the exemption.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The challenge assumed 'broke' was written to limit when the burglar is exempt. The answer says 'broke' was written for the second half of the משנה, where killing him is forbidden. There, even breaking the barrel (not just taking it) makes him liable. So the משנה's wording does not hurt רב.

keyTerms.meaning: there is blood-guilt for him (killing him counts as murder)

phrases.english: The same is true even if he took it as well,
and the fact that it teaches 'he broke the barrel'

phrases.aramaic: קָא מַשְׁמַע לַן דְּכִי יֵשׁ לוֹ דָּמִים,
phrases.english: teaches us that when there is blood-guilt for him,
phrases.notes: This is the second half of the משנה: a case where killing the burglar is forbidden.

phrases.aramaic: אַף עַל גַּב דְּשִׁיבֵּר נָמֵי – חַיָּיב.
phrases.english: even though he broke it, he is also liable.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא from step 14 by giving the משנה's wording a different purpose.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reassigning the purpose of a word in the משנה
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'Broke' was written to show that the burglar is exempt only when he broke the item.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'Broke' was written to teach that a burglar who may not be killed is liable even for breaking the item.

steps.title: Why teach this? He is obviously a damager
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the משנה needs to say this. Anyone who breaks something must pay for it.
steps.simpleTranslation: That's obvious! He is a person who caused damage!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the answer from step 15. It says the lesson it gave is too obvious to need teaching.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If killing the burglar is forbidden, he faces no death penalty, so nothing exempts him from paying. Breaking a barrel is plain damage, and every damager pays. So why would the משנה bother to say it?

phrases.english: It is obvious! He is a damager!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer of step 15 as teaching something obvious.
steps.kashyaTarget: The explanation that 'broke' teaches liability when there is blood-guilt.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Every damager pays, so the משנה would be teaching nothing new.

steps.title: Liable even when he broke it by accident
steps.stepSummary: The new lesson is that he must pay even if he broke the barrel without meaning to.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is what it teaches us: he is liable even if he broke it unintentionally.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the 'it's obvious' challenge. It points to a new detail: the breaking may have happened by accident.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Someone might think an accidental breaking does not make a person pay. The answer says the משנה teaches that he pays even then.

phrases.english: This is what it teaches us:
that even if it was unintentional.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָא קָא מַשְׁמַע לַן דַּאֲפִילּוּ שֶׁלֹּא בְּכַוָּונָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 16 by finding a new point in the משנה.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case to find a new point
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The lesson is just that a damager pays, which is obvious.
steps.terutzMaskana: The lesson is that he pays even for accidental breaking.

steps.title: We already know a person is always liable
steps.stepSummary: Accidental damage is already covered by a ברייתא: a person is always 'forewarned' and pays even for accidents.
steps.simpleTranslation: What does it teach us? That a person is always considered forewarned? We already learned this: a person is always forewarned, whether he acted by mistake or on purpose, whether by accident or willingly!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the answer from step 17. A ברייתא already teaches that people pay even for accidental damage.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule of אדם מועד לעולם means a person always pays in full for damage he causes, even by accident. Since a ברייתא already says this, the משנה would have no new reason to mention 'broke'.

keyTerms.meaning: a person is always considered forewarned, meaning fully liable for damage he causes
by accident beyond his control / willingly

phrases.english: What does it teach us?
That a person is always forewarned?
phrases.notes: 'Forewarned' means he always pays full damages, like an ox known to gore.

phrases.english: We already learned: A person is always forewarned,
whether by mistake or on purpose,
whether by accident or willingly!

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי קָא מַשְׁמַע לַן? אָדָם מוּעָד לְעוֹלָם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges step 17 by showing its lesson is already taught elsewhere.
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer that the משנה teaches liability for accidental breaking.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A ברייתא already states the rule of אדם מועד לעולם, so the משנה would be repeating it.

steps.title: The difficulty stays unanswered
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא admits it has no answer. The משנה's wording remains a difficulty for רב.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is a difficulty.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא closes this exchange by admitting the question has no answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'קשיא' here means the challenge stands and no answer is given. The משנה's word 'broke' stays a problem for רב's ruling that the burglar is exempt even when he took the items. This does not formally overturn רב's ruling.

keyTerms.meaning: it is a difficulty (the question stays unanswered)

steps.confusionAlert: 'קשיא' is different from 'תיובתא'. 'קשיא' leaves a difficulty open; it does not declare רב's view rejected.

phrases.english: It is a difficulty.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Ends the exchange started in step 14 without a final answer.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The inference from the משנה's word 'broke' remains an unanswered difficulty for רב.

steps.title: Stealing a purse on שבת: liable
steps.stepSummary: רב ביבי בר אביי quotes a ברייתא: a person who steals a purse on שבת must pay, because the theft happened before he broke שבת.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב ביבי בר אביי raised an objection: One who steals a purse on שבת is liable to pay, because he became liable for the theft before he came to break the prohibition of שבת.
steps.whatsHappening: A new challenge begins, this time against רבא. This first part of the ברייתא sets up the case that will matter in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally, if one act brings both a death penalty and a money payment, the person is exempt from paying. Here he pays because the theft (lifting the purse) came first, and breaking שבת (carrying it out) came later. So they are two separate moments.

keyTerms.meaning: the prohibition of doing forbidden work on שבת

phrases.english: Rav Beivai bar Abaye raised an objection:
One who steals a purse on Shabbat is liable,
since he already became liable for the theft
phrases.notes: He became a thief the moment he lifted the purse, while still inside.

phrases.english: before he came to the prohibition of Shabbat.
phrases.notes: Breaking שבת happens only when he carries the purse out to the public area.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new challenge, this time aimed at רבא's view from step 10.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's ruling that the burglar must return items that still exist.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Setup only: it shows the rule that money liability is cancelled only when it comes at the same moment as the death penalty.

steps.title: Dragging the purse out: exempt
steps.stepSummary: If he dragged the purse out instead of lifting it, the theft and the שבת violation happen at the same moment, so he is exempt from paying. This challenges רבא.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he was dragging it and going out, he is exempt, because the prohibition of theft and the prohibition punished by stoning come together at the same moment.
steps.whatsHappening: This is where רב ביבי's challenge lands. When the theft and the death-penalty sin happen together, the thief is exempt, even though the purse still exists.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Dragging does not make him a thief until the purse leaves the owner's property. That is the exact moment he breaks שבת. Because he is exempt here even though the purse still exists, the ברייתא seems to go against רבא, who said items that still exist must be returned.

keyTerms.meaning: dragging it along and going out
a sin punished by stoning (here, breaking שבת)

steps.whatToRemember: A money payment is cancelled only when it comes at the very same moment as a death-penalty sin. Lifting the purse makes him liable to pay; dragging it out makes him exempt.

phrases.english: If he was dragging it and going out, he is exempt,
since the prohibition of theft and the prohibition punished by stoning
come together at once.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the ברייתא started in step 20 and lands the challenge.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's ruling that a thief facing death must still return items that exist.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The dragging thief faces death at the moment of theft and is fully exempt even though the purse exists, which seems to go against רבא.

steps.title: The ברייתא is talking about a purse thrown into a river
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers the challenge against רבא. The ברייתא that exempts the thief is talking about a case where he threw the purse into a river, so it no longer exists.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the rule is: the ברייתא is talking about a case where he threw the purse into a river.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge from step 21. It explains that the ברייתא exempting the thief is talking about a purse he threw into a river.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא holds that if the stolen item still exists, the thief must give it back, even when he is exempt from paying money. The ברייתא exempted the thief who dragged the purse, which seemed to go against רבא. Now the גמרא says the ברייתא means the purse is gone, so there is nothing left to return, and רבא's rule still stands.

keyTerms.meaning: And the rule is. Here it introduces how the case should be understood.

phrases.english: And the rule is: where he threw them into a river.
phrases.notes: This means the ברייתא is talking about a purse that was destroyed, so there is nothing left to give back.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge against רבא raised in step 21.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the case: the ברייתא is about an item that no longer exists.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא seemed to exempt the thief even when the purse still exists, which goes against רבא.
steps.terutzMaskana: The exemption only means he does not pay for a destroyed item. If the item still exists, he must return it.

steps.title: רבא refuses to take back his stolen rams
steps.stepSummary: Burglars stole rams from רבא and later returned them. He refused to accept them, out of respect for רב's ruling that a burglar acquires what he stole.
steps.simpleTranslation: Burglars broke in and stole rams from רבא. They brought them back to him, but he would not take them. He said: since this ruling came out of רב's mouth, I will not take them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a story. רבא refused to take back his own stolen rams because רב had ruled that a burglar acquires what he steals.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב held that a burglar, who may be killed, acquires the stolen items, because a person who is liable with his life does not have to pay. רבא himself held that an item that still exists must be returned. Even so, he acted strictly in his own case and refused to take back the rams, so that he would not hold onto something that might belong to the burglar according to רב.

phrases.english: Rava had rams stolen from him by burglars breaking in.
They returned them to him,
but he did not accept them.
He said: Since it came out of Rav's mouth.
phrases.notes: He means רב's ruling that a burglar acquires what he stole, so the rams might now belong to the thieves.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A story that shows how seriously רבא treated רב's ruling, even after defending his own view.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבא acted strictly and refused stolen items returned by burglars, out of respect for רב's view.

steps.title: First ברייתא: the 'sun' means clear knowledge, and if unsure do not kill
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא explains that 'the sun rising upon him' is a picture of clarity. If it is clear as the sun that the burglar is dangerous, you may kill him. If it is not clear, you may not.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: 'There is no blood for him. If the sun has risen upon him.' Did the sun rise only on him? Rather, it means: if it is clear to you as the sun that he is not at peace with you, kill him. If not, do not kill him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new topic with a ברייתא about the burglar. It explains that the 'sun' in the פסוק is a picture for something being clear.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The sun rises on everyone, so the פסוק cannot simply mean 'in the daytime.' The ברייתא reads it as: when it is crystal clear that the burglar means to kill you, you may kill him. When you are unsure, killing him is forbidden.

keyTerms.meaning: There is no blood for him: killing him does not count as murder
Peace. Here it means peaceful intentions.

steps.confusionAlert: Here 'דָּמִים' (blood) means guilt for spilling blood. 'אֵין לוֹ דָּמִים' means the one who kills the burglar is not guilty of murder.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
"There is no blood for him.
If the sun has risen upon him."
But did the sun rise only upon him?

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא, אִם בָּרוּר לְךָ הַדָּבָר כַּשֶּׁמֶשׁ
phrases.english: Rather, if the matter is as clear to you as the sun
that he is not at peace with you, kill him;
and if not, do not kill him.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן אֵין לוֹ דָּמִים אִם זָרְחָה הַשֶּׁמֶשׁ עָלָיו
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new discussion about the burglar, now about when he may be killed.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: You may kill the burglar only when it is clear he intends harm. If it is unclear, it is forbidden.

steps.title: Second ברייתא: if unsure, you may kill him
steps.stepSummary: Another ברייתא reads the same picture of the sun the other way. Only if it is clear that the burglar is peaceful is killing him forbidden. If it is unclear, you may kill him.
steps.simpleTranslation: Another ברייתא teaches: 'If the sun has risen upon him, there is blood for him.' Did the sun rise only on him? Rather, it means: if it is clear to you as the sun that he is at peace with you, do not kill him. If not, kill him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second ברייתא that explains the same פסוק. It reads the sun as a picture of clarity too, but it puts the clarity on the other side.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the clear case is a peaceful burglar, such as a father who would never hurt his son, and only then is killing forbidden. Anything less than clear peace allows the homeowner to kill. This sets up a contradiction with the first ברייתא about the unclear case.

keyTerms.meaning: There is blood for him: killing him counts as murder

phrases.english: Another [ברייתא] teaches:
"If the sun has risen upon him, there is blood for him."
But did the sun rise only upon him?
Rather, if it is as clear to you as the sun

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁיֵּשׁ לוֹ שָׁלוֹם עִמְּךָ – אַל תַּהַרְגֵהוּ,
phrases.english: that he is at peace with you, do not kill him;
and if not, kill him.

steps.triggerLanguage: תַּנְיָא אִידַּךְ אִם זָרְחָה הַשֶּׁמֶשׁ עָלָיו דָּמִים לוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives an opposite reading of the same metaphor from step 24.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Killing the burglar is forbidden only when it is clear he is peaceful. If it is unclear, it is allowed.

steps.title: The two ברייתות contradict each other in the unclear case
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא points out that the two ברייתות disagree about what to do when the homeowner is unsure of the burglar's intentions.
steps.simpleTranslation: There is a difficulty: the unclear case in one ברייתא contradicts the unclear case in the other.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא raises a contradiction between the two ברייתות it just quoted. The answer will come next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both ברייתות agree on the clear cases. In the unclear case, the first says 'do not kill' and the second says 'kill.' The גמרא needs to explain how both can be right.

keyTerms.meaning: The unclear case, where nothing is known for sure

phrases.english: The unclear case contradicts the unclear case!
phrases.notes: The 'unclear case' means when you don't know the burglar's intentions. The first ברייתא forbids killing him, and the second allows it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Compares steps 24 and 25 and finds that they contradict each other.
steps.kashyaTarget: The two ברייתות about the burglar
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Both read the same פסוק as a metaphor, but they reach opposite rulings when the homeowner is unsure of the burglar's intentions.

steps.title: The גמרא begins to answer the contradiction
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא says the contradiction between the two ברייתות is not difficult. This sets up the explanation that follows.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is not difficult.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is starting to answer the contradiction from step 26 by saying 'it is not difficult.' This line only sets up the answer, and the actual explanation comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 26, one ברייתא said that when it is unclear, you may not kill the burglar, and the other said you may. Saying 'לא קשיא' tells us the גמרא will show the two ברייתות are talking about different situations. That way both can be correct.

keyTerms.meaning: It is not difficult. This is the standard opening when the גמרא is about to show that two sources do not really contradict each other.

phrases.english: It is not difficult,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens the answer to the contradiction raised in step 26 between the ברייתות of steps 24 and 25.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Resolving a contradiction by showing the two sources deal with different cases. Only the opening formula is stated here.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The two ברייתות give opposite rulings for the same unclear case.
steps.terutzMaskana: The contradiction is not real. The details of how the cases differ come in the next line.
